EVA-Bench includes 213 scenarios across three enterprise domains, a controlled perturbation suite for accent and noise robustness, and multi-trial measurements that distinguish peak from reliable capability.
EVA-Bench evaluates agents through fully automated bot-to-bot conversations.
Conversations failing any check are automatically regenerated, ensuring that evaluation scores reflect agent behavior rather than simulator artifacts.
EVA-Bench introduces a perturbation suite that varies user acoustic and behavioral conditions independently.
To our knowledge, this is the only metric in any end-to-end voice agent benchmark that evaluates the quality of the agent's spoken output at the audio level.

a conversation passes on accuracy if (Task Completion = 1.0) ∧ (Faithfulness ≥ 0.5) ∧ (Speech Fidelity ≥ 0.95) and passes on experience if (Turn-Taking ≥ 0.8) ∧ (Conversation Progression ≥ 0.5) ∧ (Conciseness ≥ 0.5).
at least one of k trials passes, measuring ceiling performance
The difference between pass@k and pass^k quantifies the gap between ceiling (peak) and consistent (reliable) performance.
We evaluated 12 systems in total: seven cascade, two hybrid, and three S2S.
Under the clean (unperturbed) condition, systems were evaluated on all 213 scenarios with k = 5 trials per scenario.
We additionally evaluated under three perturbation conditions: French-accented user speech, coffee shop background noise, and both combined.
perturbed evaluations used a randomly sampled subset of 90 scenarios (30 per domain) with k = 3 trials per scenario.

Accented speech drove the largest accuracy failures: cascade Task Completion dropped by a mean 10 points (worst system: 17 points), while no S2S model showed significant accuracy degradation (0/27 model-metric pairs).

Across all cascade systems, mean transcription accuracy on key entities was strongly correlated with mean Task Completion (Pearson r = 0.93, p = 0.002) and the relationship held within each domain (r = 0.88–0.93, all p < 0.01).

While the best-performing cascade and S2S systems achieved comparable accuracy, experience quality diverges sharply along architecture lines, with the S2S–cascade gap on EVA-X driven almost entirely by turn-taking.
EVA-Bench is released as a fully open-source, extensible framework.

Our evaluation covered 12 systems across three architectural classes, but this sample size precludes broad inferential claims about model classes.
EVA-Bench assumes that bot-to-bot simulation with a validated user simulator constitutes a valid proxy for real caller interactions.

The simulator also does not systematically generate interruptions, meaning EVA-Bench under-stresses turn-taking robustness and cannot fully differen-
tiate systems that handle barge-in gracefully.
LLM-based judges may exhibit stylistic biases, systematically favoring outputs resembling their training distribution.
Full reproduction requires access to commercial model APIs.
All tools use a declarative mock executor rather than live APIs; while schemas reflect real-world APIs, mocks cannot capture failure modes, latency variance, partial responses, or schema drift.

Customers calling a customer-service line to rebook disrupted flights — IRROPS rebooking, voluntary changes, cancellations, and vouchers.
Healthcare workers calling HR for benefits, scheduling, leave, and policy questions.
Employees calling IT support to resolve enterprise IT and service-management issues.
EVA-Bench is an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that orchestrates bot-to-bot audio conversations and scores them on both task accuracy and interaction experience.

This release contains 213 scenarios across 3 enterprise voice domains — airline customer service, healthcare HR, and IT service management — focused on situations where speaking to a human agent over the phone is realistic and necessary.

Each scenario consists of a user goal specifying the user’s intended outcome with explicit constraints … a user persona defining speaking style, patience, and personality, a scenario database containing the data the agent’s tools query and modify, and a ground truth specifying the expected database state after successful task resolution.
The Airline CSM domain covers 50 scenarios across seven workflow categories backed by 15 tools.
